title: Why Don't You See the Hole in Your Vision?
description:
There's a hole in your vision, in each eye, all the time: the optic disc, where about a million nerve fibres leave the eye and no light sensors fit. It sits 12–15° to the side of where you look and is about 5.5° × 7.5°, wide enough to hide at least ten full Moons. You never notice it because your two eyes cover for each other and your brain fills the gap with whatever surrounds it. Try the test at the start.

subtitles: Close your left eye.
Look at the cross with your right eye, and slowly move closer to the screen.
At one point, the dot on the right disappears.
Not dims.
Disappears.
There's a hole in your vision, in each eye, all the time.
So why have you never noticed it?
The answer says a lot about what seeing really is.
Light enters your eye and lands on the retina, a thin sheet of light sensors lining the back of the eye.
Rods for dim light, cones for colour.
About 90 million rods, and 4.5 million cones, in each eye.
But the retina is wired backwards.
The sensors face away from the light, and the nerve fibres that carry their signals run across the front.
To leave the eye, about 1 million of those fibres bundle together into the optic nerve.
And they punch through the retina at one spot.
That spot, the optic disc, has no light sensors at all.
It isn't tiny.
Your blind spot sits roughly 12 to 15 degrees to the side of where you're looking.
It's roughly 5 degrees wide and 7 degrees tall.
That's wide enough to hide at least 10 full Moons, side by side.
It was first described in the 1660s by the French physicist Edme Mariotte.
Not every eye is built like this.
An octopus eye is wired the other way round, with the nerve fibres behind the sensors.
So an octopus has no blind spot at all.
Ours is a side effect of how the vertebrate eye developed.
So why don't you see the hole?
Reason one: you have two eyes.
Each eye's blind spot lands on a part of the world the other eye can see.
Reason two: even with one eye closed, your brain doesn't show you a black hole.
It fills the gap with whatever surrounds it.
Stripes continue.
Colours spread.
A pattern simply carries on.
The neuroscientist V.
S.
Ramachandran showed how convincing this is.
Draw a line with a gap, and place the gap inside the blind spot.
Many people see the line as unbroken.
Here's an even bigger gap you never notice.
Sharp, detailed vision comes from a tiny patch in the centre of your eye, called the fovea.
It covers only about 2 degrees, roughly your thumbnail held at arm's length.
Everything around it is blurry, and much poorer at colour.
Yet the whole room looks sharp, because your eyes keep jumping, and your brain stitches the pieces together.
Your brain fills things in all the time.
When your eyes jump, about 3 times a second, it hides the blur.
When you move, it predicts what you're about to feel.
What you see isn't a raw camera feed.
It's your brain's best guess, built from what it expects.
So the hole has always been there.
You've just never been shown it.
Go back to the start, try the test again, and tell me in the comments:
at what distance did the dot vanish for you?
